title: Displacement-Talbot self-imaging prints periodic cell arrays without projection optics
idea: Effect: Talbot self-imaging. A periodic phase mask lit at 193 nm re-images itself at Talbot planes; sweeping the mask-wafer gap (displacement Talbot) averages out depth sensitivity and prints 36-40 nm-pitch honeycomb landing-pad and storage-node arrays across a full field in one flash. Only the aperiodic periphery goes to a scanner, and dummy rows at the array edge absorb the Talbot edge defects.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): the core array is ~51% of the die and perfectly periodic, so 1-2 of the 5-7 EUV layers move to a ~$3-5M mask-aligner-class tool; claimed 30-50% lower litho cost for those layers.

title: Oblique ion-sputter ripples self-organize sub-pitch word-line gratings
idea: Effect: Bradley-Harper sputter instability. 500 eV Ar+ ions hitting a hardmask 60-70 degrees off normal grow ripples with a 20-30 nm period on their own, and a coarse ArF pre-pattern at 4x that period pins the ripple phase and direction (guided self-organization). The ripples are transferred as the word-line grating, replacing SAQP's spacer deposition and etch loops with one broad-beam step.
why: Fact 4: SAQP takes ~12-16 steps per layer; one broad-beam ion step could cut that layer's cost ~60% with no EUV. Ripple defectivity is the open risk.

title: Million-tip field-emitter array writes periphery maskless in proximity mode
idea: Effect: Fowler-Nordheim tunneling. A wafer-scale array of gated Si or CNT tips, each with its own CMOS driver, flies 2-5 um above the resist; each tip writes only its own 50 um patch, so no electron column is needed, and sub-1 kV electrons keep proximity blur low. A digital data path replaces the periphery mask set.
why: Removes the $10-20M mask set per node and the EUV need for periphery layers (periphery ~49% of die, fact 7); makes design spins and low-volume U.S. production cheap.

title: Kirkendall voiding hollows solid pillars into double-sided cylinder capacitors
idea: Effect: nanoscale Kirkendall effect. Fill capacitor molds with solid Co or Ni pillars and sulfidize them: metal diffuses outward faster than sulfur diffuses inward, leaving a hollow tube. An H2 reduction and a thin TiN overcoat then make both inner and outer walls electrode area. This drops the double-sided cylinder flow's support-mesh litho, mold strip and extra liner deposition.
why: Fact 1 charge wall: ~1.8x electrode area at the same AR, so AR 60 behaves like ~105, and 3-5 fewer steps per capacitor module.

title: Dealloyed nanoporous electrodes multiply capacitor area inside shallow holes
idea: Effect: dealloying (selective dissolution plus surface-diffusion coarsening). Deposit a Ru-Al or Ti-Al alloy liner in a low-AR (~15:1) hole and dissolve the Al to leave a bicontinuous porous electrode with 10-20 nm ligaments; then ALD a thin high-k and a top TiN. Surface area per footprint rises 4-6x.
why: Fact 1: reaching 5 fF without AR 60-75 removes HAR mold etch and pattern-collapse controls, which are among the costliest capacitor-module tools.

title: Hydrogen-anneal surface migration forms stacked silicon-on-nothing tiers for 3D DRAM
idea: Effect: surface-energy-driven Si migration in H2. Etch a lattice of deep holes with periodic diameter modulation (scallops), then anneal in H2 at ~1100 C: surface diffusion closes each scallop into a flat buried void, giving several single-crystal Si sheets separated by empty plates (multi-layer silicon-on-nothing). Filling the voids with oxide yields 3D DRAM tiers without a 100+ layer Si/SiGe epitaxial superlattice.
why: Fact 2: the epi superlattice is the costliest and most defect-prone 3D DRAM module; an etch plus anneal could save ~$300-600 per wafer and remove strain-warpage limits on tier count.

title: Repeated smart-cut transfers stack single-crystal transistor tiers with donor reuse
idea: Effect: hydrogen-platelet exfoliation. Implanted H forms a cleave plane, so 100-200 nm single-crystal Si layers are bonded and split one at a time onto a cold DRAM wafer; each tier's lateral access transistors are patterned before the next bond. Donor wafers are re-polished and reused 10+ times.
why: Facts 2 and 3: single-crystal channels have a smaller leakage tail than deposited poly or oxide, the SiGe epi superlattice goes away, and donor reuse saves silicon and HP-quartz-crucible capacity.

title: Monolayer doping reaches buried lateral transistors in 3D DRAM tiers
idea: Effect: self-limiting chemisorption plus solid-source diffusion. Implanters cannot reach sidewalls 20 tiers down, so flood the slit with a phosphonic- or boronic-acid monolayer that bonds to every exposed Si surface, cap it, and spike-anneal to drive 3-5 nm abrupt junctions. One wet step dopes all tiers at once.
why: Fact 2: lateral-transistor doping blocks 26+ tier 3D DRAM; replaces N tilted implant passes with one wet-bench step and removes ~$8M implanters from the line.

title: Strain-driven self-rolling membranes form Swiss-roll capacitors without deep etch
idea: Effect: strain-gradient self-rolling. Put a pre-strained SiNx/TiN/HfO2/TiN stack on a sacrificial Ge strip in each lateral 3D DRAM cell; releasing the strip lets built-in strain roll the stack into a 4-6 turn micro-roll inside the tier cavity, multiplying capacitor area with no vertical etch.
why: Facts 1 and 2: the lateral capacitor blocks 3D DRAM; the rolled shape gives ~5x in-plane area with zero extra litho.

title: NbO2 Mott threshold switch replaces the access transistor in BEOL crosspoint
idea: Effect: insulator-metal (Mott/Peierls) transition. An NbO2 two-terminal selector in series with a MIM capacitor is stacked in crosspoint arrays above logic at 2 masks per layer; a sub-threshold hold bias limits leakage and refresh runs in bursts.
why: Capital: no front-end transistor per bit, 4F2 per layer, and 8 layers on cheap BEOL tools. Honest trade: Mott selector off-current is far above 13 fA, so retention is us-ms and this fits a cache or buffer tier.

title: Magnetostrictive actuators correct nanoimprint template distortion in situ
idea: Effect: magnetostriction. Galfenol or Terfenol-D thin-film actuators along the imprint template frame are driven by a coil array under the chuck, deforming the template by nanometers without contact to correct magnification and trapezoid errors field by field, with hysteresis compensation in the controller.
why: Fact 4: overlay is what keeps NIL from replacing EUV on DRAM layers; sub-2 nm overlay would move 2-3 layers to NIL at ~1/3 the EUV cost of ownership.

title: Photochromic absorbance-modulation layer lets i-line steppers print 30 nm features
idea: Effect: reversible photochromism. A diarylethene layer over the resist is held opaque by a ring-shaped 325 nm standing wave, while 365 nm light bleaches and passes only a sub-diffraction central aperture (absorbance modulation). Recycled i-line steppers with a dual-wavelength illuminator then print dense contact arrays at 30-40 nm.
why: Fact 4: used i-line tools cost ~$1-3M versus ~$200M for EUV; could remove 1-2 EUV exposures on the periodic array contact layers.

title: Layer-by-layer perovskite nanosheets give k-200 dielectric for shallow capacitors
idea: Effect: giant 2D dielectric polarizability plus electrostatic self-assembly. Alternate dips in polycation and exfoliated Ca2Nb3O10 or Sr2Nb3O10 nanosheets (k ~200 at ~10 nm) coat low-AR holes at room temperature. With k about 5x that of ZrO2 stacks, 5 fF fits in a ~12-15:1 hole.
why: Fact 1 asks for k ~70; this beats it, so AR drops from 60-75 to ~15 and the HAR etch, support mesh and collapse-control steps go away. Room-temperature wet processing on cheap tools.

title: Vapor-liquid-solid growth builds vertical access channels upward instead of etching
idea: Effect: eutectic-droplet (VLS) epitaxy. Al or Sn catalyst dots (CMOS-safe, not Au) on buried bitlines grow epitaxial Si nanowires; the liquid droplet confines growth to a 10-15 nm vertical channel already aligned to its bitline, which then gets a gate-all-around wrap for 4F2 vertical-channel DRAM.
why: Fact 4: 4F2 cuts cell area 33% versus 6F2 without a node shrink; channel diameter is set by catalyst volume rather than litho, and the damaging HAR pillar etch disappears.

title: Coulomb-blockade nanocrystal chains as a spin-coated ultra-low-leakage access switch
idea: Effect: Coulomb blockade. A vertical chain of 3-5 sub-2 nm Si nanocrystals with 1 nm SiO2 shells, spin-coated from colloid into a via, forms a multi-tunnel junction whose off state is held by a single-electron charging energy above 10 kT at room temperature; a gate lowers the blockade to write the capacitor.
why: Facts 3 and 4: leakage is set by charging energy rather than dopant precision, and the ~20-mask access-transistor FEOL is replaced by BEOL-stackable cells; claimed 100x smaller leakage tail if dot sizes stay uniform.

title: Pyroelectric domain masters print charge patterns like nanoscale xerography
idea: Effect: pyroelectricity. A LiTaO3 master is written once by e-beam domain poling; a 10 K heat pulse then raises surface charge only on the patterned domains, which picks up charged 10 nm hardmask nanoparticles electrostatically and transfers them to the wafer. The master is reused millions of times.
why: Fact 4 and masks: an optics-free, contact-light patterning tool under ~$5M for periodic array hardmask layers, with the master written only once.

title: Dielectrophoresis drops pre-made capacitor rods into transistor-wafer sockets
idea: Effect: dielectrophoresis. Coaxial TiN/ZrO2/TiN capacitor nanorods are batch-made off-wafer by template electroplating and ALD, released into a fluid, and trapped one per socket by an AC field between bitline-contact electrodes, then anneal-bonded in place.
why: Separates the most capital-heavy module (the HAR capacitor) from the FEOL fab, and batch rods cost cents per wafer-equivalent. Placement yield must exceed 99.9999%.

title: Thermophoretic wafer shielding allows ISO-7 cleanrooms for DRAM fabs
idea: Effect: thermophoresis. Every exposed wafer is held 10-20 K warmer than the gas around it inside sealed carriers and tool mini-environments; the thermophoretic force pushes sub-100 nm particles away from the warm surface, cutting deposition velocity by more than 100x, so the ballroom can be ISO 7 instead of ISO 3-4.
why: Capital: cleanroom and facilities are ~20-30% of a $15B fab and a large energy load; a cheaper shell could save billions and about a year of U.S. fab construction.

title: Electromagnetic cold-crucible Czochralski eliminates Spruce Pine quartz crucibles
idea: Effect: Lorentz-force melt levitation (cold-crucible induction). Grow 300 mm Si boules from a segmented water-cooled copper crucible in which high-frequency eddy currents hold the melt off the walls, while a cusp magnetic field damps convection. Oxygen for gettering comes from a small consumable silica rod instead of a full crucible.
why: Scarce-resource chokepoint: Spruce Pine supplies >80% of HP quartz crucibles; this removes that dependency and the crucible consumable cost.

title: Rayleigh-Plateau breakup converts one line pattern into dot arrays
idea: Effect: Rayleigh-Plateau capillary instability. Print a single 1D grating of thin amorphous-Si or Cu lines, then anneal: each line breaks into droplets at a fixed wavelength (~4.5x the line diameter), and shallow notches printed by the same mask pin the droplet positions. One litho step yields a 2D landing-pad or node array instead of two crossed patterning passes.
why: Fact 4: honeycomb pad and node layers use crossed double or quad patterning; merging the two passes saves an EUV or SAQP pass per layer, ~10-15% of array litho cost.

title: Ion-irradiation defines spin-Hall MRAM bits magnetically without stack etching
idea: Effect: irradiation-induced interface intermixing plus the spin Hall effect. Deposit a blanket MTJ stack on a W or BiSb spin-Hall write line, then irradiate through a stencil with low-dose He+ or Ar+, which intermixes CoFeB/MgO and kills perpendicular anisotropy everywhere except the bits. Bits switch by spin-orbit torque from the in-plane spin Hall current, with no MTJ etch at all.
why: Capital and yield: MTJ ion-beam etch with redeposition is MRAM's yield and cost killer; a planar, etch-free flow saves ~3 masks and the IBE tools, making SOT working memory cheaper to build in the U.S.

title: Stress-limited oxidation self-equalizes pillar diameters from sloppy cheap litho
idea: Effect: stress-retarded oxidation at high curvature. Pattern Si pillars with relaxed, high-LWR ArF or imprint litho, then wet-oxidize at ~850 C: compressive stress at small radii slows oxidation, so all pillars converge to a uniform 8-10 nm core whatever their starting diameter. Strip the oxide to get uniform vertical channels.
why: Facts 3 and 4: channel-diameter spread feeds the leakage tail; a physics-based CD equalizer lets patterning with 3x worse CD control still reach tight Vt distributions.

title: Swift heavy-ion latent tracks etch 200:1 capacitor holes in one wet step
idea: Effect: latent-track etching. A thick SiO2 or polymer mold is exposed to MeV-GeV heavy ions through a stencil with one aperture per cell; each ion leaves a damaged track that etches ~1000x faster than bulk in dilute HF, so every hole etches straight to AR 200:1 at once. Several tracks per aperture merge into one hole.
why: Fact 1: the AR ~115 needed for more charge is beyond plasma etch; a cyclotron beamline (already used roll-to-roll for track-etched membranes) replaces fleets of $10M+ cryo HAR etchers. A 40 nm-pitch stencil is the main risk.

title: Used Blu-ray mastering lasers write 40 nm imprint masters by heat-mode
idea: Effect: thermal-threshold nonlinearity. Buy two retired 405 nm Blu-ray mastering rigs (~$150k each), swap the spindle for a used XY air-bearing stage, and coat masters with a phase-change resist (AgInSbTe or Ge-Sb-Te): only the center of the Gaussian spot passes the crystallization threshold, so ~40 nm marks are written and then wet-etched selectively. The rest of the $1M funds 24 months of DRAM-array NIL master demos.
why: Masks and capital: e-beam-written NIL masters cost $0.5-1M+ each; a ~$400k heat-mode writer cuts master cost >10x and gives the U.S. its own master supply.

title: Hard-disk flying heads carry plasmonic lenses for near-field array lithography
idea: Effect: surface-plasmon near-field focusing. Bowtie plasmonic apertures on surplus HDD air-bearing sliders fly 10-20 nm above a spinning 100 mm resist-coated wafer and squeeze 355 nm light into ~25 nm spots; 16 heads write periodic cell arrays in parallel. Budget: ~$400k mechanics and lasers, $300k university fab time, $300k team over 24 months.
why: Fact 4: shows sub-30 nm patterning built from mass-produced HDD parts costing dollars each, versus a $200M EUV tool; scaling to thousands of heads is the follow-on.

title: Arrhenius rebinning sells retention-reject DRAM into temperature-guaranteed liquid-cooled racks
idea: Effect: thermally activated (Arrhenius) junction leakage, with retention roughly doubling every ~10 C cooler. Buy retention-downgraded DRAM parts at scrap prices, screen them on a ~$250k rig at 45 C and 64 ms refresh, and ship them only on liquid-cooled CXL memory modules whose controller firmware enforces a hard 50 C ceiling and throttles above it. $1M covers the rig, firmware and qualification within 24 months.
why: Raises usable supply with zero fab capital: if even 1-2% of world output is downbinned for retention, recovering it equals the output of part of a multi-billion-dollar fab.

title: High-pressure deuterium anneal heals leakage tails in downgraded DRAM wafers
idea: Effect: isotope-hardened dangling-bond passivation. Buy downgraded or scrap DRAM wafers from brokers before dicing and anneal them at ~400 C in a used 10-20 atm D2 furnace (~$400k): deuterium passivates the interface and GIDL trap centers behind the leakage tail, and Si-D bonds are ~10x more stable than Si-H. Re-test and resell recovered dies; the rest of the $1M funds test and 24 months of qualification.
why: Fact 3: trims the <=13 fA tail that sets refresh failures; recovered dies add supply with no new fab.

title: Beaker-anodized alumina provides lithography-free capacitor molds on test wafers
idea: Effect: field-assisted oxide dissolution that self-organizes pores. Sputter 3 um of Al on a transistor test wafer and anodize twice in oxalic or sulfuric acid to grow hexagonal pores at 40-60 nm pitch and AR >60:1 with zero litho; a shallow imprinted pre-texture registers pores to cells, then ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN. Budget: ~$60k electrochemical stations, ~$500k ALD and university fab time, plus the team.
why: Facts 1 and 4: HAR capacitor molds without capacitor-layer litho or HAR plasma etch, the two costliest tools in the module; validates 5 fF cells for under $1M.

title: Silver-catalyzed chemical etching makes vertical channel pillars in a wet bench
idea: Effect: metal-assisted chemical etching. A Ag mesh templated by block copolymer sits on Si; in HF/H2O2 the catalyst sinks straight down by local oxidation and dissolution, carving 10-15 nm pillars at AR >50:1 at room temperature with no plasma damage. Ag is stripped in nitric acid and residues are gettered. $1M covers wet benches, TXRF/SIMS contamination checks and 4F2 vertical-transistor test arrays.
why: Fact 4: a ~$100k wet bench replaces $8-15M HAR Si plasma etchers for 4F2 DRAM, and damage-free sidewalls may also shrink the leakage tail.

title: Backside-illuminated photoelectrochemical etch digs 150:1 trench capacitors in n-silicon
idea: Effect: photoelectrochemical macropore growth (Lehmann). In n-Si under anodic bias in HF, only holes photogenerated by backside light reach the pore tips, so pores grow straight to AR 150:1 from pits printed by i-line litho. A ~$40k PTFE cell with an LED array and potentiostat on 150 mm wafers demonstrates deep-trench DRAM capacitors within 24 months.
why: Fact 1: reaches AR far beyond 115 with a $40k tool instead of a $10M cryo etcher; fits embedded, legacy-node and chiplet DRAM at >=200 nm pitch, a niche the U.S. can manufacture.

title: Hot-wire sweep zone-anneals block copolymers into defect-free arrays
idea: Effect: directional ordering in a moving thermal gradient (zone annealing). A heated wire or line-focused IR lamp crosses a BCP film at um/s, and domains order like a directional solidification front that pushes defects to the edge, reaching long-range order in minutes instead of hours in an oven. A $40k sweeper plus ~$600k of university fab time tests 14 nm half-pitch bitline gratings.
why: Fact 4: defectivity kept DSA out of DRAM; below 0.01 defects/cm2, DSA could replace SAQP passes at ~1/5 the cost.

title: Electrochromic gel images leaky storage nodes across a whole wafer
idea: Effect: electrochromic ion insertion. Before the capacitor is built, cover the exposed storage-node contacts of a test wafer with a WO3 electrochromic gel film and bias the substrate: nodes with leaky junctions pass current that darkens the film above them, so a $20k camera maps the leakage tail of millions of cells in one integrated exposure. $1M builds the test structures, gel and optics over 24 months.
why: Fact 3 and test capital: retention test takes hours on $3-5M testers; optical whole-wafer inline screening could cut that cost >5x and give fast feedback to process tuning.

title: Water-droplet capillary self-alignment stacks DRAM dies without thermocompression bonders
idea: Effect: surface-tension energy minimization. Pattern hydrophilic pads inside hydrophobic surrounds on the dies; a coarse, ~$150k used pick-and-place drops each die onto a water film, and capillary force pulls it to <1 um alignment within ~100 ms before direct bonding. A 24-month, $1M program demonstrates 4-high wide-I/O stacks.
why: Fact 6: HBM stacking uses $3-5M TCB or hybrid bonders with slow per-die alignment; parallel capillary alignment could cut stacking capex per unit ~5-10x.

title: Shape-memory NiTi microsprings close warped HBM gaps on heating
idea: Effect: martensitic shape-memory recovery with thermal hysteresis. Sputter NiTi micro-bumps trained as compressed springs; heating above the austenite finish temperature makes each bump extend 1-3 um to meet its pad and absorb die warpage, and the hysteresis keeps them extended at operating temperature. $1M covers the target, university MEMS line time and a 24-month reliability demo.
why: Fact 6: warpage forces costly TCB and CMP-flat hybrid bonding with 20-30% yield loss; compliant self-actuating bumps raise stack yield on cheaper bonders.

title: Moire-fringe overlay upgrade lets used contact aligners reach 5 nm alignment
idea: Effect: moire magnification. Pairs of slightly mismatched gratings on mask and wafer produce fringes that magnify misalignment ~1000x; a $5k camera reads them and drives a closed-loop piezo stage retrofitted to a ~$100k used proximity aligner or imprint tool, giving sub-5 nm overlay for array layers. $1M funds two retrofits and 24 months of overlay qualification.
why: Fact 4: overlay is the barrier to cheap patterning; ~$250k per tool versus $50-200M scanners.

title: Electrohydrodynamic jet printing wires staircase DRAM stacks without TSVs
idea: Effect: electrohydrodynamic Taylor-cone jetting. Stack standard DDR dies in an offset staircase and e-jet print 1-2 um silver or copper nanoparticle traces down the stepped edges, forming hundreds of wide-I/O channels per die without through-silicon vias. $1M buys a commercial e-jet printer (~$200k), dies and 24 months of reliability work.
why: Fact 6: TSVs drive HBM's ~3x wafer area per bit and its yield loss; edge-wired stacks reuse ordinary DDR wafers and add high-bandwidth supply without TSV capex.

title: Solid-state laser interference prints 38 nm half-pitch gratings on a benchtop
idea: Effect: two-beam optical interference. Build an immersion Lloyd's-mirror interferometer with a ~$120k 213 nm fifth-harmonic Nd:YAG and a high-index prism; the fringes give about 38 nm half-pitch over a cm2 field, stepped and stitched across 100 mm wafers, and a double exposure at 60 degrees gives honeycomb arrays. $1M covers optics, resist and university fab access.
why: Fact 4: shows array layers can be printed by a <$300k tool, the first step toward a dedicated interference array-layer printer for U.S. fabs.

title: Home-built atmospheric spatial ALD deposits capacitor high-k without vacuum
idea: Effect: self-limiting chemisorption separated in space. A gas-bearing head keeps precursor and oxidant zones apart with N2 curtains, so the ALD half-reactions happen as the wafer moves under it at atmospheric pressure, depositing ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 at ~10x the rate of temporal ALD. $1M funds two heads, precursors and 24 months of electrical tests on capacitor molds.
why: Capital: vacuum ALD tools cost $3-5M; an atmospheric tool at ~$300k with higher throughput cuts deposition cost of ownership. Conformality in HAR holes is the risk.

title: Hydrogen backside gas replaces helium for wafer cooling in etch chucks
idea: Effect: gas-gap thermal conduction, set by molecular speed and the accommodation coefficient. H2 carries heat about as well as or better than He at the same low pressure, so retrofit a refurbished etch chamber's electrostatic chuck with a low-pressure H2 backside line, leak detection and N2-diluted exhaust, then qualify wafer-temperature uniformity. $1M covers the chamber and 24 months of tests.
why: Helium chokepoint: Qatar's ~30% of supply has been offline since March 2026, and backside cooling is a major fab helium use; H2 can be made on site by electrolysis.

title: Notch-guided crack propagation cuts sub-10 nm isolation gaps without cut masks
idea: Effect: controlled brittle fracture. Deposit a brittle, tensile SiNx film and use cheap i-line litho to place micro-notches; cracks start at the notches and run straight along designed stress channels, leaving 5-10 nm gaps that become word-line or active-area cuts. $1M on 150 mm wafers over 24 months measures straightness and placement accuracy.
why: Fact 4: DRAM cut and trim layers need EUV or multiple patterning; crack-defined cuts give sub-10 nm gaps from i-line tools, saving an EUV layer if placement holds.

title: Marangoni flow planarizes 3D DRAM tiers without chemical-mechanical polishing
idea: Effect: thermocapillary (Marangoni) flow. Spin a flowable siloxane and scan a laser line that sets up a surface-tension gradient, so liquid flows from hot high spots into cooler trenches and levels the topography before UV cure. A ~$250k scanned-laser coater on 100 mm wafers tests planarity over 26-tier stair topography within 24 months.
why: Fact 2: 3D DRAM tier stacks need many CMP steps ($5M tools, slurry, defects); thermocapillary leveling could replace a share of them.

title: Ultrasonic piezo excitation speeds nanoimprint resist fill several-fold
idea: Effect: piezoelectric ultrasonic excitation (acoustic streaming and shear thinning). A transducer behind the imprint template drives 20-100 kHz vibration that speeds capillary filling of nanoscale cavities and dissolves trapped gas, cutting fill time per field from ~1 s to ~0.2 s. A ~$400k retrofit of a used imprint tool plus a 24-month defect study.
why: Fact 4: NIL throughput (~25 wafers/hour per head) and bubble defects limit it as an EUV substitute; faster fill raises throughput and cuts litho cost per layer.

title: Superionic silver-sulfide stamps electrochemically etch metal lines without resist
idea: Effect: solid-state ion migration in a superionic conductor. A Ag2S stamp patterned once is pressed onto a Ag or Cu film under bias, and Ag+ ions move into the stamp only at contact points, removing metal with ~10 nm fidelity with no resist and no plasma etch. $1M demonstrates bitline-pitch metal patterning on 100 mm wafers.
why: Fact 4 and capital: one stamp station replaces coat, expose, develop, etch and strip for metal layers; Cu or Ag lines also avoid tungsten (~80% from China).

title: Light-addressed electrodeposition prints periphery metal from a DMD projector
idea: Effect: photoconductivity. In a plating bath, a DMD projector lights a photoconductive a-Si:H or TiO2 seed layer, making only the lit pixels conductive, so copper deposits in the projected pattern with no mask or resist. $150k of optics plus ~$700k of development reaches 1-2 um lines for periphery and redistribution layers in 24 months.
why: Facts 6 and 7 and masks: maskless metal for periphery and packaging RDL cuts mask and litho cost for low-volume U.S. DRAM and fast design spins.

title: Capillary condensation fills only narrow array gaps, eliminating block masks
idea: Effect: capillary condensation (Kelvin equation). Below saturation, a precursor vapor such as a silazane condenses only in gaps narrower than the Kelvin radius (~10-20 nm), so dense array trenches fill while wide periphery stays open; a cure turns the liquid into oxide. $1M tests the effect on test arrays at university fabs within 24 months.
why: Fact 4: each array/periphery block mask removed saves a litho plus etch pass; Kelvin-selective fill could drop 1-3 block masks per flow.

title: Joule self-heating crystallizes each tier's channel through its own wordline
idea: Effect: localized Joule heating. Deposit amorphous Si channels in every 3D DRAM tier, then send a microsecond current pulse through each lateral strip so only that strip melts and recrystallizes (self-aligned electrical annealing) while lower tiers and BEOL stay cold. A $1M program on 100 mm wafers with 4-tier stacks measures grain size and leakage in 24 months.
why: Fact 2: low-thermal-budget single-grain channels block 3D DRAM; pulse generators replace $10M+ excimer laser annealers.
